newsitem.title: USA: Wall Street shares seen tilting down at open.
newsitem.headline: Wall Street shares seen tilting down at open.

text.p: Wall Street is seen opening flat to slightly lower on Thursday, with defensive, blue-chip shares coming under pressure after Nike Corp's announcement its quarterly earnings would be below forecast.
Technology stocks, which comprise a large part of the Nasdaq composite index and which have been strong performers lately, might also see some profit-taking at the market open.
"The bias could be slightly down this morning, with the classic favorites of defensive buyers coming under pressure," said Joseph Battipaglio, chief investment officer at Gruntal.

Nike said it expected fourth quarter earnings for the fourth quarter ending May 31 of $0.51 to $0.56 per share, including a one-time $0.04 per share charge, below analysts' consensus estimates of $0.69 per share.
The company said its revenues would be below analysts' estimates for the quarter amid shifts in order mix, shipment timings, product shortages and order cancellations.
"This could spook investors and have a visible effect on the Dow," Battipaglio said. "This is a tried-and-true company which has disappointed."
Other analysts said while the Nike announcement could hurt other sneaker makers, it would not necessarily drag down the Dow more than near-term.
"It's not going to have that big an effect, though it could hurt Reebok and Fila," Larry Wachtel, an analyst at Prudential Securities, said.

The Dow industrial average closed lower on Wednesday as worries about the outlook for long-term interest rates caused investors to take profits. It finished at 7357.23 points, off 26.18, while Nasdaq inched up 0.97 points to 1410.18.
Technology stocks would be active, but share direction would depend on the firm's area of focus, analysts said.
"Not all tech stocks are homogenous," Wachtel said.
On Thursday, The Standard & Poor's 500 futures index was off 0.85 points at 850.
Analysts said stocks would continue to worry about inflation and the yield on long bond, which has risen above a key seven percent yield.
The help-wanted index could be scrutinized by the bond market, which worried about a tight labor market, Peter Cardillo, research director at Westfalia Investments said.
The long bond was trading up 3/32 at a 7.02 percent yield. The index was forecast unchanged at a reading of 87 in April.
Tokyo's 225-share Nikkei average fell 39.11 points, or 0.19 percent, to 20,312.23.
In London, the FTSE 100 was off two points at 4675.5. U.S. stocks struggled for clear direction in London.
The dollar rose against the yen in Tokyo after earlier losses were offset by slugglish Japanese output data.
It was trading at 116.20/30 yen in Tokyo and at 1.7032/42 against the mark in Europe.

The Wall Street Journal's Heard on the Street column reported that Wall Street reacted negatively to news of a proposed $10.9 billion merger between CUC International Inc and HFS Inc, still worried about each company's strategies.

The New York Times Market Place column said AT&T Corp Chairman Robert Allen has said the company needs a local telephone partner to compete in a deregulated market and that his designated heir does not need to run the combined company. The newspaper cited people familiar with AT&T's talks with SBC Communications Corp over a proposed merger.
